1	# Svalboard — Hands Down Neu + Arensito symbols
2	
3	Vial keymap for the Svalboard Lightly, ported from my Glove80.
4	
5	## Load it
6	
7	1. Open [KeyBard](https://captdeaf.github.io/keybard/) with the Svalboard plugged in.
8	2. **Load** → `SvalHandsDownNeu.vil`.
9	
10	No reflash — Vial writes the keymap live.
11	
12	Needs `/dev/hidraw*` to be readable, which it isn't by default. The udev rule is
13	in `system/etc/udev/rules.d/92-vial.rules`. Without it, KeyBard and Vial both see
14	the keyboard and then silently fail to open it.
15	
16	## Layers
17	
18	Each finger sits in a cup with five switches: **N**orth, **S**outh, **E**ast,
19	**W**est and **C**enter (the plain down-press). East is screen-right on both
20	hands, so West is inward on the right hand and outward on the left.
21	
22	### Layer 0 — Hands Down Neu
23	
24	```
25	             W    N     C     S     E
26	  L pinky    tab  w     r     x     -
27	  L ring     .    f     s     c     .
28	  L middle   (    m     n     l     v
29	  L index    g    p     t     d     b
30	  R index    ,    .     a     u     :
31	  R middle   /    q     e     o     )
32	  R ring     ;    "     i     y     &
33	  R pinky    z    '     h     k     j
34	```
35	
36	The alphas are Hands Down Neu as it sits on the Glove80 — note `;` on the right
37	inner column where upstream publishes `-`.
38	
39	Two places this departs from a literal port, both because the Svalboard has four
40	fingers per hand and the layout assumes five columns:
41	
42	- **`g` is on the index's West.** Hands Down gives the left index the whole
43	  inner column (`v`/`b`/`g`). Only two fit on an index cup, so it keeps `b` and
44	  `g` and exiles `v` — the rarest — to the middle finger.
45	- **`z`, `j` and `tab` are on laterals.** They live in outer columns the
46	  Svalboard doesn't have. `tab` gets the left pinky's West, x=0.0, the outermost
47	  point of the hand.
48	
49	Brackets are deliberately *not* on this layer; Arensito has them. Five symbols
50	*are*, placed by measured frequency rather than by feel — counted over hand-typed
51	prompts and shell history (agent-driven sessions excluded) and over code authored
52	here, per 1000 characters:
53	
54	| | `-` | `:` | `(` `)` | `&` |
55	|---|---|---|---|---|
56	| code | 11.6 | 9.3 | 4.9 | 0.68 |
57	| hand-typed | 33.5 | 5.1 | 0.30 | 0.17 |
58	
59	- `-` → **left pinky East.** The clear winner on both counts.
60	- `:` → **right index East**, the strongest free lateral. Was shift+`;`.
61	- `(` `)` → **left middle West / right middle East**, an outward-facing mirror
62	  pair, so `()` alternates hands. They earn a base key from code only.
63	- `&` → **right ring East.** The rarest thing on this layer, on the worst key
64	  here, which is the point. Ring laterals are the hardest cups to reach.
65	
66	`*` was considered and rejected: it looks like 6.7/1k in code, but 90% of that
67	is `**` in markdown prose, and it is 0.03/1k in anything hand-typed.
68	
69	Each is promoted, not copied — all five are holes on layer 1, so nothing sits on
70	two keys.
71	
72	### Layer 1 — Arensito symbols (hold `MO(1)`)
73	
74	```
75	  { } [ ] @   · · < > $
76	  ; / · 0 ·   \ 1 · · =
77	  6 7 8 9 +   * 2 3 4 5
78	```
79	
80	Ported from the Glove80 `symbols` layer. `·` is a dead key — Arensito puts
81	`-`, `:`, `&`, `_`, `(` and `)` there, and all six are one-key elsewhere now
82	(see layer 0 and the thumbs below). They're dead rather than transparent on
83	purpose: falling through would type `n`, `.`, `e`, `i`, `b` and `/` from the
84	middle of the symbol layer.
85	
86	The grid above is on N/C/S; the
87	laterals carry the six symbols Arensito leaves out, which would otherwise cost
88	`MO(1)`+shift+key:
89	
90	```
91	  ` ~ on the left pinky      ! on the left index
92	  % on the left ring         # on the left middle
93	  | on the right index       ^ on the right middle
94	```
95	
96	`?` isn't here on purpose — it's shift+`/`, and `/` is on the base layer.
97	
98	`_` gets a second seat on the **left thumb's space key**. Arensito's own `_` is
99	on the right index's North, the same hand as `MO(1)`; on space it's a
100	left-right roll instead. Space itself isn't typeable while `MO(1)` is held —
101	every other thumb stays transparent, so shift, ctrl, enter and backspace still
102	work on the layer.
103	
104	### Layer 2 — navigation (hold `MO(2)`)
105	
106	Arrows four-across on the right hand, innermost to outermost, matching Glove80
107	base-layer positions 75–78:
108	
109	```
110	  R index  R middle  R ring  R pinky
111	     ←        ↓        ↑        →
112	```
113	
114	F1–F12, home/end, pgup/pgdn, volume and play/pause fill the rest.
115	
116	### Layer 15 — mouse
117	
118	Svalboard's firmware switches here by itself when the pointing device moves, and
119	leaves on the first key that isn't on this layer. **Nothing reaches it by
120	keypress, by design.** Buttons 1/3/2 sit on index/middle/ring South of both
121	hands; `USER06` is `SV_RECALIBRATE_POINTER`.
122	
123	### Thumbs
124	
125	```
126	LEFT                                RIGHT
127	 row7  esc(7.4)  shift(8.5)  ctrl(9.6)     alt(11.4)  MO1(12.5)  MO2(13.6)
128	 row6   space(7.9) delete(9.0) gui(10.1)    enter(11.9) ralt(13.0) bspc(14.1)
129	```
130	
131	The two rows interleave in x, so every row-6 key sits between two row-7 keys —
132	and the **middle** row-6 key on each hand, x=9.0 and x=13.0, is the only
133	position with no free side. Nothing you press in a hurry goes there. `gui` was
134	there originally (on both hands) and was unusable; `tab` was tried there and was
135	worse. They now hold `delete` and `ralt`.
136	
137	`space` left and `bspc` right match Glove80 positions 69 and 74 — Svalboard's own
138	configs ship those mirrored.
139	
140	## Regenerating
141	
142	```sh
143	python3 build.py
144	```
145	
146	`build.py` emits the entire `.vil`. There is no base file to patch and no
147	network access — every layer, keycode and piece of Vial metadata is declared in
148	it. It was cut over from a patch-the-Colemak-config approach by diffing against
149	the old output until byte-identical, so the rewrite carried nothing over by
150	accident.
151	
152	Four guards, any of which aborts the build:
153	
154	- **Geometry.** `CUP_XY` holds the physical position of all 40 finger switches,
155	  read out of the keyboard's own `vial.json` over the Vial protocol. The build
156	  asserts North is above Center, South below, East right and West left, for
157	  every cup. Get the column order wrong and you still emit a structurally
158	  perfect file with every key in the wrong place — this is the check that
159	  catches it, and it checks against the hardware rather than another config's
160	  conventions.
161	- **Coverage.** All 26 letters and 10 digits reachable, plus space, backspace,
162	  enter, tab and grave. Grave has no shift-fallback and went missing once when
163	  Arensito's `{` landed on top of it.
164	- **Symbol cost.** No printable ASCII symbol may require `MO(1)`+shift+key.
165	- **Duplicates.** Nothing on the base layer reachable from two positions.
166	  Moving a key by adding an override leaves the original behind unless it's
167	  blanked; that put `g` on two cups once.
168	
169	Thumb rows are declared by physical x, not column index, and the build fails if
170	the declared positions don't match the hardware. The indices are **not** mirrored
171	between hands — left column 3 is at x=7.9 and mirrors right column *4* at
172	x=13.6, not right column 3 at x=14.1. Reasoning about them directly produced one
173	wrong answer already.
174	
175	## Source
176	
177	Glove80 layout `e3409150-bb22-49c0-8614-10035f3f6a04` ("Sauyon layout
178	2026-01-20"), layers `Base` and `symbols`. Its grids are transcribed into
179	`build.py`; nothing is fetched at build time.
180	
181	Custom `USER*` keycode names (`SV_SCROLL_TOGGLE`, `SV_TOGGLE_AUTOMOUSE`, the
182	sniper modes, DPI controls) come from the keyboard itself — Vial command
183	`0xFE 0x02` returns an LZMA-compressed `vial.json` describing them.
184

1	#!/usr/bin/env python3
2	"""Generate a Svalboard Vial keymap (.vil) for Hands Down Neu + Arensito symbols.
3	
4	Emits the whole file. There is no base .vil to patch and no network access --
5	every layer, every keycode and all the Vial metadata is declared below.
6	
7	Source of truth for the alphas and symbols is my Glove80, my.glove80.com layout
8	e3409150-bb22-49c0-8614-10035f3f6a04, layers `Base` and `symbols`. Its grids are
9	transcribed into the constants below.
10	
11	Run `python3 build.py` to write SvalHandsDownNeu.vil. The build refuses to emit
12	anything unless check_geometry() and check_coverage() both pass.
13	"""

15	import json
16	import pathlib
17	import sys
18	
19	HERE = pathlib.Path(__file__).parent
20	OUT = HERE / "SvalHandsDownNeu.vil"
21	
22	# uid identifies the physical keyboard. Read off mine over the Vial protocol
23	# (raw HID usage page 0xFF60, command 0xFE 0x00). Vial warns on a mismatch.
24	UID = 5199957870438586395
25	
26	LAYERS = 16
27	ROWS = 10
28	COLS = 6
29	
30	# --- Svalboard geometry ------------------------------------------------------
31	#
32	# layout[layer] is 10 rows x 6 columns.
33	#
34	#   row 0 = left thumb cluster      row 5 = right thumb cluster
35	#   rows 1-4 = left  index, middle, ring, pinky
36	#   rows 6-9 = right index, middle, ring, pinky
37	#
38	# A finger row's first five columns are the five switches of that cup, in
39	# absolute directions -- East is screen-right on both hands. Column 5 is unused
40	# on finger rows and must be -1; thumb rows use all six.
41	
42	S, E, C, N, W = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4
43	
44	L_THUMB, R_THUMB = 0, 5
45	L_INDEX, L_MIDDLE, L_RING, L_PINKY = 1, 2, 3, 4
46	R_INDEX, R_MIDDLE, R_RING, R_PINKY = 6, 7, 8, 9
47	
48	THUMB_ROWS = (L_THUMB, R_THUMB)
49	FINGER_ROWS = (L_INDEX, L_MIDDLE, L_RING, L_PINKY,
50	               R_INDEX, R_MIDDLE, R_RING, R_PINKY)
51	
52	FINGER_NAMES = {
53	    L_INDEX: "L index", L_MIDDLE: "L middle", L_RING: "L ring", L_PINKY: "L pinky",
54	    R_INDEX: "R index", R_MIDDLE: "R middle", R_RING: "R ring", R_PINKY: "R pinky",
55	}
56	DIR_NAMES = {S: "South", E: "East", C: "Center", N: "North", W: "West"}
57	
58	# Physical key positions, in KLE units, read out of the keyboard's own vial.json
59	# (Vial command 0xFE 0x02, LZMA-compressed). This is the hardware's account of
60	# itself, not a convention borrowed from some other config -- which is what
61	# makes check_geometry() below worth running.
62	CUP_XY = {
63	    L_INDEX:  {S: (9.5, 3.5),  E: (10.5, 2.5), C: (9.5, 2.5),  N: (9.5, 1.5),  W: (8.5, 2.5)},
64	    L_MIDDLE: {S: (7.0, 2.0),  E: (8.0, 1.0),  C: (7.0, 1.0),  N: (7.0, 0.0),  W: (6.0, 1.0)},
65	    L_RING:   {S: (3.5, 2.0),  E: (4.5, 1.0),  C: (3.5, 1.0),  N: (3.5, 0.0),  W: (2.5, 1.0)},
66	    L_PINKY:  {S: (1.0, 3.5),  E: (2.0, 2.5),  C: (1.0, 2.5),  N: (1.0, 1.5),  W: (0.0, 2.5)},
67	    R_INDEX:  {S: (14.5, 3.5), E: (15.5, 2.5), C: (14.5, 2.5), N: (14.5, 1.5), W: (13.5, 2.5)},
68	    R_MIDDLE: {S: (17.0, 2.0), E: (18.0, 1.0), C: (17.0, 1.0), N: (17.0, 0.0), W: (16.0, 1.0)},
69	    R_RING:   {S: (20.5, 2.0), E: (21.5, 1.0), C: (20.5, 1.0), N: (20.5, 0.0), W: (19.5, 1.0)},
70	    R_PINKY:  {S: (23.0, 3.5), E: (24.0, 2.5), C: (23.0, 2.5), N: (23.0, 1.5), W: (22.0, 2.5)},
71	}
72	
73	# Thumb keys, same source. Reason about these by x, never by column index -- the
74	# indices are NOT mirrored between hands (left col 3 at x=7.9 is the mirror of
75	# right col 4 at x=13.6, not right col 3 at x=14.1).
76	THUMB_XY = {
77	    L_THUMB: {4: (7.4, 7.0), 3: (7.9, 6.0), 2: (8.5, 7.0),
78	              5: (9.0, 6.0), 0: (9.6, 7.0), 1: (10.1, 6.0)},
79	    R_THUMB: {0: (11.4, 7.0), 1: (11.9, 6.0), 2: (12.5, 7.0),
80	              5: (13.0, 6.0), 4: (13.6, 7.0), 3: (14.1, 6.0)},
81	}

83	# --- Alpha block placement ---------------------------------------------------
84	#
85	# A layout's alpha block is 3 rows x 5 columns, written the way layouts always
86	# are: outward-in on the left hand, inward-out on the right.
87	#
88	#   left:  pinky ring middle index inner      right: inner index middle ring pinky
89	#
90	# The Svalboard has four fingers per hand and no inner-index column, so the
91	# inner column spills onto one inward-facing lateral per finger. That lateral is
92	# East on the left hand and West on the right.
93	
94	INNER_LATERAL = {"top": "middle", "home": "index", "bottom": "ring"}
95	
96	
97	def place(block, hand):
98	    """Map a 3x5 alpha block onto {(row, col): keycode} for one hand."""
99	    if hand == "left":
100	        rows = {"pinky": L_PINKY, "ring": L_RING, "middle": L_MIDDLE, "index": L_INDEX}
101	        cols = ["pinky", "ring", "middle", "index"]
102	        inner_col, lateral = 4, E
103	    else:
104	        rows = {"pinky": R_PINKY, "ring": R_RING, "middle": R_MIDDLE, "index": R_INDEX}
105	        cols = ["index", "middle", "ring", "pinky"]
106	        inner_col, lateral = 0, W
107	
108	    out = {}
109	    for i, finger in enumerate(cols):
110	        col = i if hand == "left" else i + 1
111	        out[(rows[finger], N)] = block["top"][col]
112	        out[(rows[finger], C)] = block["home"][col]
113	        out[(rows[finger], S)] = block["bottom"][col]
114	
115	    for band, finger in INNER_LATERAL.items():
116	        out[(rows[finger], lateral)] = block[band][inner_col]
117	
118	    return out
119	
120	
121	# --- Layer 0: Hands Down Neu -------------------------------------------------
122	#
123	#   w f m p v   / . q " ' z
124	#   r s n t b   , a e i h j
125	#   x c l d g   ; u o y k
126	#
127	# As it sits on the Glove80, including `;` on the right inner column where
128	# upstream Hands Down Neu publishes `-`.
129	
130	HDNEU_LEFT = {
131	    "top":    ["KC_W", "KC_F", "KC_M", "KC_P", "KC_V"],
132	    "home":   ["KC_R", "KC_S", "KC_N", "KC_T", "KC_B"],
133	    "bottom": ["KC_X", "KC_C", "KC_L", "KC_D", "KC_G"],
134	}
135	
136	HDNEU_RIGHT = {
137	    "top":    ["KC_SLASH", "KC_DOT", "KC_Q", "LSFT(KC_QUOTE)", "KC_QUOTE"],
138	    "home":   ["KC_COMMA", "KC_A", "KC_E", "KC_I", "KC_H"],
139	    "bottom": ["KC_SCOLON", "KC_U", "KC_O", "KC_Y", "KC_K"],
140	}
141	
142	# The Glove80's outer column (z, j) and its bottom row (grave, backslash,
143	# brackets) have no Svalboard equivalent -- those are columns this keyboard
144	# doesn't have. They go on the spare laterals, openers left and closers right.
145	BASE_LATERALS = {
146	    (R_PINKY, W): "KC_Z",    # inner, x=22.0
147	    (R_PINKY, E): "KC_J",    # outer, x=24.0
148	    # Hands Down Neu publishes `-` on the right inner column; this port puts `;`
149	    # there, following the Glove80. That evicts `-`, and `-` is far too frequent
150	    # -- kebab-case, `->`, `--flag` -- to sit behind MO(1). It gets a lateral.
151	    (L_PINKY, E): "KC_MINUS",
152	    (L_PINKY, W): "KC_TAB",    # outermost key on the left hand, x=0.0
153	
154	    # Parens likewise: frequent enough in code to be worth a base-layer key
155	    # rather than MO(1)+key.
156	    #
157	    # They were on the left ring's two laterals, which is the wrong pair. The
158	    # ring laterals are the hardest keys on this board to hit -- that is a
159	    # verdict from typing on it, and the only kind available: CUP_XY is KLE
160	    # layout units, so it can say where a key is drawn but nothing about the
161	    # reach. Nothing frequent goes on a ring lateral.
162	    #
163	    # The middles' outer laterals are the strongest free pair instead, and they
164	    # mirror: West is outward on the left hand, East outward on the right. That
165	    # also makes `()` alternate hands rather than roll along one.
166	    (L_MIDDLE, W): "LSFT(KC_9)",
167	    (R_MIDDLE, E): "LSFT(KC_0)",
168	
169	    # `:` takes the index's East, the strongest free right-hand lateral. It is
170	    # the most frequent symbol that still costs two keys: ~9 per 1000 chars of
171	    # code written here, and that survives context-checking -- 47% of it is
172	    # `key: value` in yaml/json/nix and 16% slices and ternaries, against only
173	    # 27% prose colon. It was shift+`;`, so this saves one keystroke, the same
174	    # win the parens got.
175	    (R_INDEX, E): "LSFT(KC_SCOLON)",
176	
177	    # `&` is the opposite case and lands on a ring lateral deliberately: 0.68
178	    # per 1000 in code, 0.17 in hand-typed text, the rarest thing on the base
179	    # layer. The ring laterals are the worst keys here, which is exactly what a
180	    # symbol this rare should be occupying. It stays on the right hand, where
181	    # Arensito had it.
182	    (R_RING, E): "LSFT(KC_7)",
183	
184	    # In Hands Down the left index owns the entire inner column -- v, b and g
185	    # are all index-finger keys. INNER_LATERAL has to scatter them, because a

194	    #
195	    (L_INDEX, W): "KC_G",

# Code Review

## Overview

**They find, you fix.** Follow the spirit, not the letter: dispatching a
reviewer satisfies the letter; one that read an empty diff, or that you never
waited for, looked at nothing and found nothing. The rule is that
somebody who did not write the change has said what is wrong with it — and that
cannot be you. You read the change you meant to make, not the one on disk.

**Write for the agent who inherits this: the next phase agent is you, with your
context gone.** A finding you settled in your head is one they meet as a bug,
with nothing saying anyone saw it.

## The Iron Law

```
NO CHANGE IS DONE UNTIL A READ-ONLY REVIEWER HAS SEEN IT AND
EVERY CRITICAL AND IMPORTANT FINDING IS RESOLVED OR RECORDED AS DEFERRED.
```

**Read-only** is a trust boundary, not a performance note: the reviewer reads
anything, runs read-only checks, and writes nothing — not source, not git, not
run state. You stay the single writer.

No exceptions:

- **Never run a reviewer in the background.** Do not set `run_in_background`,
  do not yield, and do not schedule a wakeup while one is out. A backgrounded
  reviewer parks you mid-turn, indistinguishable from a finished turn, and the
  run stalls until a human nudges the pane. Dispatch it blocking and read its
  verdict in the turn you dispatched it.
- **Do not judge a change too small to review.** A one-line edit to a condition
  is the size this skill exists for. Dispatch a reviewer over it.
- **Do not count your own read as the review.** Re-reading your diff tells you
  it matches what you intended — the one thing never in doubt. Dispatch someone
  who does not know it.
- **Do not leave it for the pipeline's review phase.** That phase reads what you
  hand it, after later work is built on it. Dispatch here, while the change is
  one commit wide.
- **Do not close a finding by disagreeing with it.** When you will not fix one,
  quote it and write the reason in the report or handoff. An unrecorded
  decision reads downstream like an unread finding.
- **Do not repeat a verdict you have not read.** Open the file the reviewer
  names, or re-run the review when it named none. A reviewer that never came
  back has not said "clean".

## Announce

Say this out loud before dispatching anything:

```
Using drovr:code-review — dispatching read-only reviewers before calling this done.
```

## The procedure

> When a skill or briefing gives you a numbered checklist, create **one tracked item per step**
> using whatever task tool this harness exposes — `TodoWrite`, or `TaskCreate`/`TaskUpdate` —
> before you start step 1. Mark each in-progress when you start it and complete when its
> evidence is in hand. If the harness exposes no task tool, write the checklist to
> `~/.local/share/drovr/runs/<run>/checklist.md` when inside a run, or `CHECKLIST.md` at the
> repo root otherwise, and tick items there. An untracked checklist decays with the context
> window; that decay is the exact failure drovr exists to fight.

Re-create those items for each change you review, not once for the session.

1. **Write down the change and the exact range** — the files, and `<base>..HEAD`.
   Get it wrong and the reviewer reports clean on nothing.
2. **Dispatch read-only reviewers, blocking, one per angle:** run
   `drovr code-review run <run> <task>` (`<base>` from `<task>-base.sha`, recorded
   before your first edit) — or, **inline** with no run,
   `drovr code-review run --base "$(git merge-base HEAD main)" <task>`. Nothing
   else, and never invent a run to get one.

   It spawns one reviewer per **configured** angle — `config.angles`, which
   defaults to correctness, security, error-handling, type-design — each writing
   `<task>-review-<angle>.json`, merged into `<task>-review.json`. **Read the
   config, not this page**, and cover any lens it omits yourself.

   Tell each reviewer to review as a skeptic, not the author; to say whether the
   tests exercise the behaviour, not just that they pass; to rate every finding
   **Critical, Important or nit** — what the Iron Law gates on — and say so when
   it found none; and to write them to a path you name, so step 3 has something
   to open. The lenses to cover:
   - **Spec compliance** — what was agreed, no more, no less?
   - **Correctness** — real bugs, unhandled cases, broken invariants.
   - **Verification** — do the claimed tests exist, and would they fail on a
     regression?
   - **Quality** — reuse, simplification, consistency with the code around it.
3. **Wait for every reviewer, then read what each wrote.** Open the findings
   file by path. Exit codes: 0 clean, 3 findings, 2 timeout, 1 error — **only 0
   is clean**, and a reviewer that returned no verdict is none of the four.
   Re-dispatch rather than report its silence.
4. **Check what the reviewer actually read — range *and* working tree.** The
   range must be the whole of `<base>..HEAD`, every file you touched, not a
   subset you picked; **and uncommitted work is in scope, not exempt** — drovr's
   panel reviews the diff *plus the current working tree*. A verdict covers what
   is on disk only if the reviewer saw both. Clean on an empty range, a subset,
   or a tree with unreviewed edits in it is about a change nobody read.
5. **Resolve every Critical and Important finding, or record the deferral.**
   Per finding: quote it, then name the edit answering it by file or write down
   why you are not making it.
6. **Re-run the checks after your last review-driven edit, then say it is
   done.** The fixes are new, unverified code: run the tests. When the change is
   not code and has no suite, name what you re-read instead and why it covers the
   edits — written down, never assumed. Report the findings, the edits and the
   deferrals; inside a drovr phase this also gates `drovr phase done`.

## Requirements

The middle column is what the claim takes; the right is what gets accepted
instead.

| The claim | Required evidence | NOT sufficient |
|---|---|---|
| *"This change has been reviewed"* | A read-only reviewer dispatched over this change in the foreground, returned in this turn, and the range you handed it, written down | Your own re-read · a reviewer launched and not waited for · a review of the tree before your last edit |
| *"The reviewer found nothing"* | The findings file it wrote, opened by path and read by you — or the review re-run by you when it wrote none — **and** what it read shown to be the whole of `<base>..HEAD` **plus your working tree** | Its summary, however much output it pastes · exit 1 or 2 · a subset of your files · uncommitted edits nobody looked at · a verdict that never arrived |
| *"Every Critical and Important finding is resolved"* | Each quoted, the edit answering it named by file, and step 6's checks re-run after the last edit | A count · agreeing with one in prose · fixing the Criticals and leaving the Importants |
| *"That finding does not apply here"* | The finding quoted, and the reason written where the next agent reads it | Deciding it in your head · *"out of scope"* with no scope named · silence, which downstream reads as resolved |

## Red flags — STOP

Some are thoughts, some are things you have just written. Either way you are at
the line.

- *"They are going to read it line by line anyway."* · *"The lead said just
  send it."* · *"It is a two-line change."* · *"I already reviewed it myself."*
  · *"The pipeline's review phase will catch it."* — each opens a row in
  *Rationalizations*, verbatim. Go do the thing in its row.
- *You are about to launch a reviewer in the background and keep working.* →
  Dispatch it blocking. No version of that ends with you reading its verdict
  this turn.
- *A reviewer has not come back and you are writing the report.* → Block on it.
  Silence is not a pass; a parked reviewer is not a finished one.
- *The panel came back clean in seconds on a large diff.* → Check what it read.
  Clean and empty look identical from here.
- **Anything that treats the change as finished** — any wording at all, and
  also committing, opening a PR, or starting the next task — while a reviewer is
  unread, unreturned, or holding an unresolved Critical or Important finding. If
  you cannot name the reviewer and point at what it wrote, change what you
  dispatched, not how you word it.

## Rationalizations

The right column is an instruction, not an argument. Do the thing in it.

| The thought | Do this instead |
|---|---|
| *"They are going to read it line by line anyway."* | Dispatch the reviewer first, then send it. Two different reads: theirs is for fit, the review's is for correctness, and one does not make the other redundant — reading a document aloud catches prose gaps, not retry semantics. |
| *"The lead said just send it."* | Send it after the review, and tell them the call moves. That is a scheduling reflex, not anyone weighing the technical risk — the calendar is theirs, the correctness yours. |
| *"It is a two-line change."* | Dispatch a reviewer over the two lines. Size is not a risk measure, and the risk you estimate in order to skip the review is what it would have told you. |
| *"I already reviewed it myself."* | Dispatch one that did not write it. Your read confirms the diff matches your intent; the defects worth catching are in what you did not think of. |
| *"The pipeline's review phase will catch it."* | Dispatch here, now. That phase reads what you hand it, after later tasks built on it; a finding costs more at every step it survives. |
| *"The reviewer came back with no findings."* | Open the file it named, and check it read your whole change, working tree included. An empty range comes back clean from every angle at once. |

## Worked example

Condensed from a real decision: a 320-line spec, a client call in 19 minutes
where three people read it aloud, a $45,000 sign-off, the lead writing
*"just send it."* Reviewer output is illustrative, not a transcript.

❌ **What this looks like when it fails:**

> They are going to read it out loud section by section — that *is* the review,
> and a review pass first is a second reading of something nobody has read
> once. The lead said send it. Sending.

✅ **What it looks like when it holds:**

> Using drovr:code-review — dispatching read-only reviewers before calling this
> done. The "second reading" framing conflates two reads: theirs is for fit,
> the review's is for correctness, and one does not make the other redundant.
> "Just send it" is a scheduling call; the retry semantics are mine. Moving the
> call:

```
$ drovr code-review run warehouse-sync spec
reviewed 320 lines (a41c9e2..HEAD) · 4/4 angles returned
correctness    IMPORTANT §4.2 retry window (30s) < the 45s ack timeout in §3.1
error-handling IMPORTANT §6 reconciliation excludes the partial-day boundary
type-design    nit       §2 names two ids for one endpoint
exit 3
```

> Both Importants fixed in `spec/warehouse-sync.md` — retry window 30s → 60s, §6
> reconciliation now spans the boundary day — from `spec-review.json`, not the
> summary line. A spec has no suite, so step 6 here is both edited
> sections re-read against §3.1, not assumed. The nit is deferred
> and recorded here: the duplicate id is in a section the client wrote, and
> renaming it would confuse the walkthrough. Sent 22 minutes late, call moved:
> that window would have shipped a contract we could not meet.

# Targeted mDNS service query -- the mechanism printers advertise on. No network
# scanning: one multicast question, listen for answers.
import socket, struct, sys, time

SERVICES = ["_ipp._tcp.local", "_ipps._tcp.local", "_printer._tcp.local",
            "_pdl-datastream._tcp.local", "_uscan._tcp.local"]

def encode_name(name):
    out = b""
    for label in name.split("."):
        out += bytes([len(label)]) + label.encode()
    return out + b"\x00"

def query(names):
    hdr = struct.pack("!6H", 0, 0, len(names), 0, 0, 0)
    body = b"".join(encode_name(n) + struct.pack("!HH", 12, 1) for n in names)  # PTR/IN
    return hdr + body

def decode_name(data, off):
    parts, seen = [], 0
    while True:
        if off >= len(data): break
        ln = data[off]
        if ln == 0:
            off += 1; break
        if ln & 0xC0 == 0xC0:
            ptr = struct.unpack("!H", data[off:off+2])[0] & 0x3FFF
            if seen > 20: break
            seen += 1
            sub, _ = decode_name(data, ptr)
            parts.append(sub); off += 2; break
        parts.append(data[off+1:off+1+ln].decode("utf-8", "replace"))
        off += 1 + ln
    return ".".join(p for p in parts if p), off

s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
s.setsockopt(socket.IPPROTO_IP, socket.IP_MULTICAST_TTL, 2)
s.bind(("0.0.0.0", 0))

=== system/deploy ===
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Run as your normal user (e.g. `mise run deploy`), NOT under sudo: the sops
# steps below decrypt with your GCP key under $HOME and each privileged install
# sudo's itself. Running the whole script as root points $HOME at /root, so sops
# can't find the key (and root has no KMS creds) -- fail fast instead.
if [ "$(id -u)" -eq 0 ]; then
  echo "system/deploy: run as your user (try 'mise run system:deploy'), not root." >&2
  exit 1
fi

cd "$(dirname "$0")"
find etc/ -type d | while read -r d; do sudo mkdir -p "/${d}"; done
find etc/ -type f | while read -r f; do sudo cp -v "${f}" "/${f}"; done

# polkit only scans /usr/share/polkit-1/actions for action definitions, which
# etc/ can't reach; install Bitwarden's unlock action there so its "system
# authentication" biometric prompt is authorized on this non-NixOS host.
sudo install -Dvm644 polkit-1/actions/com.bitwarden.Bitwarden.policy \
  /usr/share/polkit-1/actions/com.bitwarden.Bitwarden.policy

# ── gnome-keyring: let the home-manager unit own the daemon ───────────────────
# The login collection can only be unlocked at daemon startup, so home-manager
# runs its own gnome-keyring.service whose ExecStart unseals the passphrase from
# the TPM (see gnome-keyring-tpm in home.nix). Mask Arch's packaged units so a
# second, *locked* daemon can't be started behind our back -- its socket unit
# listens on %t/keyring/control and would socket-activate one on any control-op.
# This is only half the job: the D-Bus activation files in /usr/share also start
# a locked daemon, and systemd masking does nothing about those. They are
# shadowed from ~/.local/share/dbus-1/services by home.nix.
sudo rm -f /etc/systemd/user/sockets.target.wants/gnome-keyring-daemon.socket
sudo ln -sfn /dev/null /etc/systemd/user/gnome-keyring-daemon.socket
sudo ln -sfn /dev/null /etc/systemd/user/gnome-keyring-daemon.service

# Unsealing the gnome-keyring passphrase reads /dev/tpmrm0, which is root:tss 0660.
# Takes effect at next login, not in the current session.
if ! id -nG "$USER" | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -qx tss; then
  sudo gpasswd -a "$USER" tss
fi

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
# systemd-oomd parses oomd.conf (and its drop-ins) once at startup, so a changed
# etc/systemd/oomd.conf.d/* must be followed by an actual restart. `enable --now`
# is NOT enough: --now only *starts* a stopped unit, so on a host where oomd is
# already running it is a silent no-op and the new limits sit on disk unapplied.
# `restart` covers both cases (starts it if stopped) and kills nothing on its way
# through -- oomd holds no state worth preserving across a reload.
sudo systemctl enable systemd-oomd
sudo systemctl restart systemd-oomd

# ── attic binary cache: make nix read nix.custom.conf + render the pull token ──
# nix.custom.conf adds attic.ko.ag/kube as an extra substituter; the cache is
# PRIVATE, so the nix daemon needs a read token. We are not a nix `trusted-user`,
# so both the config and the token must reach the daemon at the system level.
#
#   • Determinate Nix auto-`!include`s nix.custom.conf from /etc/nix/nix.conf and
#     merges /etc/determinate/netrc.custom (via config.json) into its netrc.
#   • Plain upstream nix (e.g. utsuho) does neither, so we wire it up here:
#       - ensure /etc/nix/nix.conf `!include`s nix.custom.conf (idempotent)
#       - render the token to /etc/nix/netrc, the daemon's default netrc-file
#     (On a Determinate host the extra /etc/nix/netrc copy is simply unused.)
# The token is sops-encrypted in ../secrets.yaml: decrypt as the user (GCP KMS),
# then install to /etc as root. The token is never printed.
export GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS="${GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS:-$HOME/.config/sops/gcp-key.json}"

# Plain upstream nix only reads /etc/nix/nix.conf; pull in nix.custom.conf so the
# substituter + trusted key take effect. Idempotent, and a no-op on Determinate
# (whose own nix.conf already includes it, so the grep matches and we skip).
if ! sudo grep -qF 'nix.custom.conf' /etc/nix/nix.conf 2>/dev/null; then
  echo '!include nix.custom.conf' | sudo tee -a /etc/nix/nix.conf >/dev/null
fi

sops -d --extract '["atticPullToken"]' ../secrets.yaml \
  | sed 's#^#machine attic.ko.ag password #' \
  | sudo install -m600 -o root -g root /dev/stdin /etc/determinate/netrc.custom
sops -d --extract '["atticPullToken"]' ../secrets.yaml \
  | sed 's#^#machine attic.ko.ag password #' \
  | sudo install -m600 -o root -g root /dev/stdin /etc/nix/netrc

# ── remote builder: SSH key the nix daemon uses to reach mari ─────────────────
# nix.custom.conf delegates aarch64-darwin builds to sauyon@mari-1 over Tailscale;
# the daemon (root) authenticates with this key. Private key is sops-encrypted in
# ../secrets.yaml; install root-owned, 0600. Never printed.
sops -d --extract '["mariBuilderKey"]' ../secrets.yaml \
  | sudo install -m600 -o root -g root /dev/stdin /etc/nix/mari-builder-key

# Pick up the new substituter, trusted key, netrc, and builder.
sudo systemctl restart nix-daemon

# ── tailscaled: patched build from this flake (Linux only) ───────────────────
# Tailscale SSH calls logind CreateSession before the user's shell runs, so for a
# systemd-homed user whose LUKS home is still locked it starts user@<uid>.service
# against homed's fallback home ("/") and permanently breaks that user manager's
# unit search path for the rest of the boot. The patch makes tailscaled ask homed
# for the user's state first and skip session creation when the home isn't active.
# See ../patches/tailscale-ssh-skip-logind-session-for-locked-homed-user.patch
#
# Build as the invoking user (root's nix may lack flakes and our substituters),
# then have root pin the result. A symlink placed directly in /nix/var/nix/gcroots
# is a permanent GC root, and we reuse it as the stable path tailscaled.service
# references -- it must resolve at boot, i.e. outside the encrypted home.
if [[ "$(uname -s)" == Linux ]]; then
  ts_out="$(nix build --no-link --print-out-paths "$(cd .. && pwd)#tailscale-patched")"
  sudo ln -sfn "${ts_out}" /nix/var/nix/gcroots/tailscale-patched
  # The CLI too: /usr/bin/tailscale belongs to the distro package, which this
  # replaces. The wrapper dispatches on argv[0], so a symlink named `tailscale`
  # gets CLI behaviour rather than the daemon.
  sudo install -d /usr/local/bin
  sudo ln -sfn /nix/var/nix/gcroots/tailscale-patched/bin/tailscale /usr/local/bin/tailscale
  sudo systemctl daemon-reload
  sudo systemctl restart tailscaled
fi

Base directory for this skill: /nix/store/REDACTED/skills/systematic-debugging

# Systematic Debugging

## Overview

**A fix you cannot explain is a guess wearing a diff.** Until the failure
happens on demand and you can say *mechanistically* why, any change you make is
as likely to hide the bug as to remove it. Follow the spirit, not the letter:
running the reproduction once, seeing red, and then fixing what you *assumed*
was wrong satisfies the ordering and proves nothing. The rule is that the cause
you fix is the cause you demonstrated.

**Write for the agent who inherits this: the next phase agent is you, with your
context gone.** They will not have your hunch, your scrollback, or the shape you
recognized. They get the reproduction command, the cause you wrote down, and the
test you added — anything you only knew is lost at the phase boundary.

## The Iron Law

```
NO FIX BEFORE A REPRODUCTION AND A MECHANISTIC CAUSE.
```

No exceptions:

- **Do not act on a shape you recognize.** A failure matching one you have seen
  before is a reason to *suspect* a cause, not a reason to skip confirming it.
  Go read this instance's fixture, input, or state and confirm it is that bug.
  Recognition works on the assertion output; the bug lives somewhere you have
  not looked yet.
- **Do not read a conditional instruction as permission to skip its condition.**
  *"If it's the off-by-one, just fix it"* waives re-litigating the fix once the
  cause is confirmed — it never waives confirming it. Establish the antecedent
  yourself, then take the permission it grants.
- **Do not let a deadline shorten the verification.** After the fix, re-run the
  original trigger **and** the full suite — the scope
  `drovr:verification-before-completion` defines, not one you pick under time
  pressure. The clock does not change which tests can catch what this fix
  disturbed. If the full suite genuinely cannot be run here, name the exact
  command you did not run and do not report the bug as fixed.
- **Do not start fix #4.** Three *failed fixes* — the unit is defined in step 6 —
  means your model of the system is wrong, not that the fourth guess is due.
  Stop, say so, and question the design with whoever owns it before changing
  another line.
- **Do not substitute reasoning for a reproduction.** If you cannot trigger the
  failure on demand, that is the finding to report. Keep narrowing — smaller
  input, more logging, a read-only explorer — and stop before shipping a fix
  you cannot verify.

## Announce

Say this out loud when you start, before the first edit:

```
Using drovr:systematic-debugging — reproducing before fixing.
```

## The procedure

> When a skill or briefing gives you a numbered checklist, create **one tracked item per step**
> using whatever task tool this harness exposes — `TodoWrite`, or `TaskCreate`/`TaskUpdate` —
> before you start step 1. Mark each in-progress when you start it and complete when its
> evidence is in hand. If the harness exposes no task tool, write the checklist to
> `~/.local/share/drovr/runs/<run>/checklist.md` when inside a run, or `CHECKLIST.md` at the
> repo root otherwise, and tick items there. An untracked checklist decays with the context
> window; that decay is the exact failure drovr exists to fight.

Re-create those items for each bug you work, not once for the session. If you
fall back to `CHECKLIST.md` at a repo root, do not commit it.

1. **Reproduce.** Get a reliable, minimal trigger and record the exact command
   and its output. A bug you cannot reproduce on demand is a bug you cannot
   prove you fixed.
2. **Isolate.** Narrow to the smallest input, file, or code path that still
   shows it. Bisect, add logging, or dispatch a **read-only explorer** to map
   the suspect area. Fan-out investigation belongs to read-only explorers (e.g.
   `explore-mcp`), never to parallel writers — you keep the editing, which is
   what keeps drovr's single-writer rule intact.
3. **Root-cause.** Explain *why* it happens, mechanistically. "Adding this line
   makes it go away" is not a cause. Keep going until the explanation predicts
   the observed behavior exactly — including the parts you were not chasing.
4. **Fix.** Make the minimal change that addresses the cause, not the symptom.
5. **Verify.** Re-run your original trigger and confirm it is gone, then run the
   **full suite** — unconditionally, whatever the clock says.
   `drovr:verification-before-completion` owns what "full" means here and what
   evidence it takes; do not substitute a narrower scope you picked yourself.
   Add or fix a test that would have caught it.
6. **Escalate at three failed fixes.** A **failed fix** is one change you made,
   ran, and watched leave the failure in place. That is the unit — not edits, not
   builds, not ideas you considered and dropped. Count them for this one failure.
   At three, stop and question the design with whoever owns it; do not start fix
   #4 without that conversation. A run of wrong fixes is evidence about your
   model of the system, not about the next fix.

### The cycle

```dot
digraph debugging_loop {
  rankdir=LR;
  node [shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor=white];

  repro  [label="reproduce it\non demand", shape=diamond, fillcolor=lightyellow];
  story  [label="no trigger —\nyou have a story,\nnot a bug"];
  cause  [label="mechanistic cause", shape=diamond, fillcolor=lightyellow];
  fix    [label="minimal fix,\nat the cause", fillcolor=palegreen];
  verify [label="trigger +\nthe full suite", shape=diamond, fillcolor=lightyellow];
  stop   [label="three failed fixes —\nquestion the design", fillcolor=lightpink];
  // "failed fix" is procedure step 6's unit: a change made, run, and seen to

  done   [label="fixed, with a test\nthat would have caught it"];

  story  -> repro  [label="narrow: smaller input,\nlogging, read-only explorer"];
  repro  -> cause  [label="on demand"];

  cause  -> fix    [label="predicts the\nobserved behavior"];
```

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Measure how often characters actually get typed, for keymap decisions.

The layout's symbol placements are argued from measured frequency rather than
feel (see README). This builds the corpus that argument rests on, caches it, and
reports per-1000-character rates -- so the next "should I promote X?" is one
command instead of a re-derivation.

    python3 freq.py                # refresh corpus, report the promoted set
    python3 freq.py '`' '~'        # rates for specific characters
    python3 freq.py --all          # every printable ASCII symbol
    python3 freq.py --no-refresh   # report from the cache, don't re-read sources

WHERE THE CORPUS LIVES, AND WHY NOT HERE
----------------------------------------
The cache goes in ~/.local/share/svalboard-freq/, never in this repo. This repo
is public; the corpus is shell history and prompts, which carry internal
hostnames, paths and work detail. What IS safe to commit is the aggregate --
per-1000 rates for single characters reveal nothing about content -- so freq.py
writes freq.json here and that is what the README's table is built from.

If you ever change the extraction, delete the cache rather than trusting it:
the manifest records the filters that produced it, but not their intent.

THE THREE CORPORA
-----------------
`prompts`  Text you typed to agents. Sidechains (subagent transcripts) and
           machine-injected blocks are dropped -- see EXCLUDE_PREFIXES. What
           survives is meant to be keystrokes your hands actually made, which
           is the thing a keymap should be optimised for.
`shell`    zsh history, with the `: <ts>:<elapsed>;` metadata stripped so the
           timestamps don't dilute the rates.
`code`     Text files tracked in this repo, minus generated artifacts. Counting
           a generated .vil or the rendered cheatsheet would be measuring this
           script's own output, not typing.

A rate is per 1000 characters of the corpus, so the corpora stay comparable
despite very different sizes.
"""

import argparse
import json
import pathlib
import re
import subprocess
import sys
from collections import Counter
from datetime import datetime, timezone

HERE = pathlib.Path(__file__).parent
REPO = HERE.parent.parent
CACHE = pathlib.Path.home() / ".local/share/svalboard-freq"
CORPUS_DIR = CACHE / "corpus"
MANIFEST = CACHE / "manifest.json"
AGGREGATE = HERE / "freq.json"

PROJECTS = pathlib.Path.home() / ".config/claude-work/projects"
ZSH_HISTORY = pathlib.Path.home() / ".local/share/zsh/history"

# The symbols the README argues about, in the order that table lists them.
PROMOTED = ["-", ":", "(", ")", "&"]

# Blocks that arrive in a `user` turn without anyone typing them: hook output,
# tool results rendered as text, slash-command scaffolding, system nudges. They
# are the bulk of a long transcript and would swamp the real keystrokes.
EXCLUDE_PREFIXES = (
    "<system-reminder>", "<command-name>", "<command-message>", "<command-args>",
    "<local-command-stdout>", "<local-command-stderr>", "<task-notification>",
    "<user-prompt-submit-hook>", "<session-start-hook>", "<bash-input>",
    "<bash-stdout>", "<bash-stderr>", "Caveat: The messages below",
    "[Request interrupted", "API Error", "<EXTREMELY_IMPORTANT>",
    "DROVR GATE", "<SUBAGENT-STOP>",
)

# Generated or vendored: counting these measures a generator, not a person.
CODE_SKIP = {
    "flake.lock", "SvalHandsDownNeu.vil", "cheatsheet.html", "freq.json",
    "opencode.json", "secrets.yaml",
}
CODE_SKIP_SUFFIX = {".lock", ".png", ".jpg", ".jpeg", ".pdf", ".zst", ".gz", ".vil"}


def iter_prompt_text():
    """Hand-typed user text from agent transcripts.

    Yields one string per surviving block. `find` does not work under this
    home (systemd-homed), so the transcripts are globbed.
    """
    files = sorted(PROJECTS.glob("*/*.jsonl"))
    kept = dropped = 0
    for path in files:
        try:
            raw = path.read_text(errors="replace")
        except OSError:
            continue
        for line in raw.splitlines():
            if not line.strip():
                continue
            try:
                rec = json.loads(line)
            except (json.JSONDecodeError, ValueError):
                continue
            if rec.get("isSidechain"):
                continue
            if rec.get("type") != "user":
                continue
            msg = rec.get("message")
            if not isinstance(msg, dict) or msg.get("role") != "user":
                continue

            content = msg.get("content")
            blocks = []
            if isinstance(content, str):
                blocks = [content]
            elif isinstance(content, list):
                for b in content:
                    # tool_result blocks are output, not typing.
                    if isinstance(b, dict) and b.get("type") == "text":
                        t = b.get("text")
                        if isinstance(t, str):
                            blocks.append(t)

            for text in blocks:
                stripped = text.lstrip()
                if any(stripped.startswith(p) for p in EXCLUDE_PREFIXES):
                    dropped += 1
                    continue
                kept += 1
                yield text
    print(f"  prompts: {len(files)} transcripts, {kept} blocks kept, "
          f"{dropped} machine-injected blocks dropped", file=sys.stderr)


# zsh extended history: ": <epoch>:<elapsed>;<command>", commands may continue
# onto following lines with a trailing backslash.
ZSH_META = re.compile(r"^: \d+:\d+;")


def iter_shell_text():
    if not ZSH_HISTORY.exists():
        print(f"  shell: {ZSH_HISTORY} missing, skipping", file=sys.stderr)
        return
    raw = ZSH_HISTORY.read_text(errors="replace")
    n = 0
    for line in raw.splitlines():
        cmd = ZSH_META.sub("", line)
        if not cmd.strip():
            continue
        n += 1
        yield cmd
    print(f"  shell: {n} history lines", file=sys.stderr)


def iter_code_text():
    """Text files tracked in this repo, minus generated artifacts."""
    try:
        out = subprocess.run(
            ["git", "-C", str(REPO), "ls-files", "-z"],
            capture_output=True, check=True,
        ).stdout.decode(errors="replace")
    except (subprocess.CalledProcessError, FileNotFoundError) as exc:
        print(f"  code: git ls-files failed ({exc}), skipping", file=sys.stderr)
        return

    n = 0
    for rel in out.split("\0"):
        if not rel:
            continue
        p = pathlib.Path(rel)
        if p.name in CODE_SKIP or p.suffix in CODE_SKIP_SUFFIX:
            continue
        full = REPO / p
        try:
            text = full.read_text(errors="strict")
        except (OSError, UnicodeDecodeError):
            continue  # binary or unreadable
        n += 1
        yield f"\x00PATH:{rel}\n{text}"
    print(f"  code: {n} tracked text files", file=sys.stderr)


SOURCES = {
    "prompts": iter_prompt_text,
    "shell": iter_shell_text,
    "code": iter_code_text,
}


def build_corpus():
    CORPUS_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    manifest = {
        "built": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(timespec="seconds"),
        "sources": {},
        "note": "Raw corpus. Contains shell history and prompts -- never commit.",
    }
    print("building corpus:", file=sys.stderr)
    for name, fn in SOURCES.items():
        parts = list(fn())
        text = "\n".join(parts)
        (CORPUS_DIR / f"{name}.txt").write_text(text)
        manifest["sources"][name] = {"chars": len(text), "blocks": len(parts)}
    MANIFEST.write_text(json.dumps(manifest, indent=2) + "\n")
    return manifest


def load_corpus():
    if not MANIFEST.exists():
        raise SystemExit(
            "no cached corpus -- run without --no-refresh to build it first"
        )
    out = {}
    for name in SOURCES:
        p = CORPUS_DIR / f"{name}.txt"
        out[name] = p.read_text(errors="replace") if p.exists() else ""
    return out


def rates(corpus, chars):
    """Occurrences per 1000 characters, per corpus."""
    table = {}
    for name, text in corpus.items():
        n = len(text)
        counts = Counter(text)
        table[name] = {
            c: (counts.get(c, 0) * 1000.0 / n) if n else 0.0 for c in chars
        }
        table[name]["_chars"] = n
    return table


def code_split(corpus, char):
    """Per-extension breakdown for the code corpus.

    This is the check that killed `*`: 6.7 per 1000 looked promotable until it
    turned out to be `**` in markdown prose. A symbol that lives in one file
    type is a symbol you type in one context.
    """
    text = corpus.get("code", "")
    by_ext = Counter()
    tot_ext = Counter()
    for chunk in text.split("\x00PATH:"):
        if not chunk:
            continue
        head, _, body = chunk.partition("\n")
        ext = pathlib.Path(head.strip()).suffix or "(none)"
        by_ext[ext] += body.count(char)
        tot_ext[ext] += len(body)
    return by_ext, tot_ext


def fenced_split(corpus, char):
    """For the prompts corpus: inside ``` fences vs outside.

    Backticks especially: a rate driven entirely by fenced code blocks is a
    rate driven by pasting, not by prose typing.
    """
    text = corpus.get("prompts", "")
    inside = outside = 0
    in_fence = False
    for line in text.split("\n"):
        if line.lstrip().startswith("```"):
            in_fence = not in_fence
            inside += line.count(char)
            continue
        if in_fence:
            inside += line.count(char)
        else:
            outside += line.count(char)
    return inside, outside


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__,
                                 formatter_class=argparse.RawDescriptionHelpFormatter)
    ap.add_argument("chars", nargs="*", help="characters to report (default: the promoted set)")
    ap.add_argument("--all", action="store_true", help="every printable ASCII symbol")
    ap.add_argument("--no-refresh", action="store_true", help="use the cached corpus")
    args = ap.parse_args()

    if args.no_refresh:
        corpus = load_corpus()
    else:
        build_corpus()
        corpus = load_corpus()

    if args.all:
        chars = [c for c in map(chr, range(33, 127)) if not c.isalnum()]
    elif args.chars:
        chars = []
        for a in args.chars:
            chars.extend(list(a))
    else:
        chars = PROMOTED

    table = rates(corpus, chars)

    print()
    print("per 1000 characters")
    widths = max(6, max((len(repr(c)) for c in chars), default=6))
    hdr = "  " + "corpus".ljust(10) + "".join(repr(c).center(widths + 2) for c in chars)
    print(hdr)
    print("  " + "-" * (len(hdr) - 2))
    for name in SOURCES:
        row = "  " + name.ljust(10)
        for c in chars:
            row += f"{table[name][c]:.2f}".center(widths + 2)
        print(row)
    print()
    for name in SOURCES:
        print(f"  {name}: {table[name]['_chars']:,} chars")

    # Context checks, only worth printing for a handful of characters.
    if len(chars) <= 4:
        for c in chars:
            print(f"\n  --- context for {c!r} ---")
            inside, outside = fenced_split(corpus, c)
            tot = inside + outside
            if tot:
                print(f"  prompts: {outside:,} outside ``` fences, {inside:,} inside "
                      f"({100 * inside / tot:.0f}% fenced)")
            by_ext, tot_ext = code_split(corpus, c)
            top = by_ext.most_common(5)
            if top and sum(by_ext.values()):
                s = sum(by_ext.values())
                for ext, n in top:
                    if not n:
                        continue
                    per1k = n * 1000.0 / tot_ext[ext] if tot_ext[ext] else 0
                    print(f"  code {ext:<8} {n:>6} occurrences "
                          f"({100 * n / s:>4.0f}% of all) {per1k:>6.2f}/1k in that type")

    # The publishable half: aggregate rates only, no corpus.
    every = [c for c in map(chr, range(33, 127)) if not c.isalnum()]
    agg = rates(corpus, every)
    AGGREGATE.write_text(json.dumps({
        "generated_by": "freq.py",
        "note": "Per-1000-character rates. Aggregates only -- the corpus itself "
                "is local (~/.local/share/svalboard-freq) and unpublishable.",
        "corpus_chars": {k: agg[k]["_chars"] for k in SOURCES},
        "rates": {
            k: {c: round(agg[k][c], 4) for c in every} for k in SOURCES
        },
    }, indent=2) + "\n")
    print(f"\nwrote {AGGREGATE.relative_to(REPO)} (aggregates only)")
    print(f"corpus cached in {CACHE} (local, not committed)")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())
